body: The account's ambiguity hypothesis remains the most directly grounded reading: the problem statement itself says the flatmates agree and later disagree about what the agreement meant. That is a specification gap. The rival does not refute this; it adds a second possible gap: not what the agreement meant, but whether any mutually binding agreement is wanted. The avoidance is compatible with either. So I would not choose one diagnosis. I would sequence a test that lets both show themselves. Revised plan: 1. No group meeting and no shared note yet. Talk separately to the other two, briefly, about two things: what they want the flat to be (a shared project with obligations, or overlapping private lives), and which one or two chores actually recur. Ask as a real question, not a survey. 2. Do not aggregate the answers immediately. If they diverge on what the flat is, treat that as the dispute the chores keep surfacing. If they agree, use the concrete chores. 3. Try a small trial on two or three items. Either tightened specification (what done means, by when, fallback) or a truce-shaped arrangement (owned zone, rotation with a default outcome nobody negotiates in the moment). Pick based on the conversation, not on a theory. Set a review date. 4. Watch what the withdrawing flatmate does with the proposal itself. If they engage with the content and recurrence falls, the ambiguity reading gains support. If they pull back from the very idea of a written or settled arrangement, the unit-versus-privacy reading gains support. If they disengage from both after one or two low-pressure attempts, stop optimizing chores and name the living-arrangement question. 5. Keep the ask small. Ten minutes on bins and kitchen is better than a talk about the whole house. But if the issue is the second axis, even a narrow ask can feel like the same imposition; that is why the separate conversations and the content-versus-proposal observation matter. 6. Avoid moral language, counting instances in the moment, and a single big settlement. Those convert a specification or unit question into a character dispute. What I would leave open: which reading is correct; whether load imbalance, outside stress, or conflict fatigue is the real driver; how long to persist before treating non-engagement as a signal about the lease. A review date is a practical substitute for a principled threshold, not an answer. I would reject the idea that either reading is established by this thin material, and I would reject using the rival's privacy reading as a blanket shield for not doing a fair share. The account's own objection is right that the specification move can treat a symptom; the rival's objection is right that the truce move can pathologize any attempt to make expectations explicit. Both objections should bind any plan. The selected input objection is absent, so there is no separate criticism to weigh. That absence limits confidence; it does not make the account or rival correct. The next move is small, separate, concrete, and reviewed.
